paragraphs: Bilevel optimization couples two optimization problems: the quantity being minimized depends on the solution of another problem. This creates a difficulty for large datasets. Computing an outer gradient requires solving a linear system, so using a few randomly selected examples does not straightforwardly produce an unbiased gradient estimate.

The paper introduces a framework that updates three quantities together: the inner solution, the linear-system solution, and the main optimization variable. Its update directions can be expressed as sums, making unbiased sampling possible. This organization also allows variance reduction to act across all three evolving quantities, addressing sampling noise throughout the coupled computation.

Within this framework, the authors develop SABA, an adaptation of SAGA. They prove an O(1/T) convergence rate and, under the Polyak–Łojasiewicz assumption, linear convergence. They identify these guarantees as firsts for stochastic bilevel optimization. Numerical experiments support the method's usefulness, connecting the framework's cleaner stochastic updates to a practical algorithm with convergence guarantees.
neurips-2022-a-framework-for-bilevel-opt.tldr: A joint-update framework enables unbiased stochastic bilevel optimization and variance reduction, yielding SABA with O(1/T) convergence and conditional linear convergence.

paragraphs: Best subset selection seeks a model that minimizes an empirical loss while using only a limited number of nonzero variables. This sparsity constraint makes the problem nonconvex. The paper studies how to accelerate projected gradient optimization by exploiting the structure of the feasible solutions: they form a finite collection of linear subspaces, each corresponding to a selection of variables.

The first acceleration scheme uses same-space extrapolation. It takes advantage of progress within a shared subspace to speed optimization while adding negligible computational cost. The second scheme identifies a subspace before changing optimization methods. It begins with ordinary projected gradient iterations, identifies the appropriate subspace containing an optimal solution, and then applies an efficient smooth optimizer within it.

The authors provide global convergence guarantees for both schemes and superlinear convergence for the second-stage approach. Their experiments report orders-of-magnitude speed improvements over unaccelerated methods and the state of the art. The central contribution is to use the geometry of sparse solutions to organize faster optimization.
neurips-2022-accelerated-projected-gradi.tldr: Two acceleration schemes exploit the subspace structure of sparse optimization to provide convergence guarantees and substantial empirical speedups.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning can produce representations that support classification across domains. A linear classifier trained on one domain may also classify another accurately, even when the two domains occupy distant regions of the representation space. The paper calls this linear transferability and investigates why it can happen in unsupervised domain adaptation.

The analysis focuses on how examples relate across domains. The authors prove that transferability can occur when examples belonging to the same class across domains are more related than examples belonging to different classes across domains. For instance, the relevant relationship is whether dogs in photographs connect more strongly to cartoon dogs than to cartoon cats.

The result does not require the domains to have nearby representations. The analysis permits weak relationships and unbounded density ratios between source and target data. This matters because successful transfer can depend on the organization of class relationships even when domain differences remain pronounced. The stated condition explains a route to transferability; it is not presented as a guarantee for every contrastively learned representation.
neurips-2022-beyond-separability-analyzi.tldr: Contrastive representations can support linear transfer across distant domains when cross-domain relationships favor matching classes.

paragraphs: Video understanding can benefit from knowing which objects appear, where they are, and how they interact. Obtaining these structured annotations for every frame is expensive. StructureViT investigates whether a small collection of annotated still images, available only during training and potentially from another domain, can provide useful structure for video models.

The framework adds object tokens to a transformer so that images and videos can share a representation of scene structure. A Frame-Clip Consistency loss connects the representations of individual frames with those of still images, allowing structured information to pass between image and video training. The paper instantiates this idea with a Hand-Object Graph: hands and objects have locations, and graph connections indicate contact or its absence.

The authors report strong improvements across several video understanding tasks and datasets, including first place in the stated Ego4D temporal localization challenge. The contribution is a training framework that makes limited image annotations useful for video understanding, reducing reliance on densely annotated video frames.
neurips-2022-bringing-image-scene-struct.tldr: StructureViT transfers scene structure from a small annotated image collection into video models using shared object tokens and frame-clip consistency.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning uses inputs and relationships between positively associated examples to learn representations without task labels. Many successful methods have separate theoretical explanations, making their connections difficult to see. This paper develops a shared framework through spectral manifold learning, which studies representations using the structure of relationships among data points.

The authors connect methods including VICReg, SimCLR, and Barlow Twins to spectral embedding approaches such as Laplacian Eigenmaps and ISOMAP. Within this framework, they derive closed-form optimal representations and, for linear networks, optimal network parameters. They also analyze how the chosen pairwise relationships affect these solutions and downstream task performance.

The resulting bridge connects contrastive methods with global spectral approaches and non-contrastive methods with local ones, suggesting benefits and limitations of each. One stated consequence is conditional: when training relationships align with the downstream task, all the SSL methods in the analysis produce representations optimal for that task. This highlights the choice of relationships as a central part of designing useful self-supervised training.
neurips-2022-contrastive-and-non-contras.tldr: A spectral-learning framework connects contrastive and non-contrastive methods and explains how training relationships shape their optimal representations.

paragraphs: Self-training uses a model's predictions on unlabeled data to help train that model further. Much of this work targets overall accuracy. Practical systems may instead need objectives such as improving the lowest recall across classes. Such a goal depends on performance across groups of predictions and cannot be treated simply as independent correctness on each example.

The paper introduces Cost-Sensitive Self-Training, or CSST, to extend self-training to these non-decomposable metrics. Its purpose is to make the use of unlabeled examples serve the chosen performance objective. The authors prove that the framework can better optimize the desired metric using unlabeled data under distributional assumptions similar to those used in existing self-training analyses.

The framework also yields practical deep-learning methods for vision and language tasks with different non-decomposable objectives. Experiments show improvements over the state of the art in a majority of the tested dataset-and-objective cases. These results support tailoring self-training to the operational metric, while preserving the qualification that improvements were not reported for every case.
neurips-2022-cost-sensitive-self-trainin.tldr: CSST extends self-training to non-decomposable performance goals, with conditional theoretical support and improvements in most tested cases.

paragraphs: Optimization algorithms can favor particular solutions even without an explicit penalty specifying that preference. This implicit regularization helps explain the models that training produces. The paper asks whether adding momentum changes that preference, focusing on linear classification where the data are separable and the loss has an exponential tail.

For this setting, the authors prove that gradient descent with momentum converges to the same L2 maximum-margin solution as ordinary gradient descent. This solution separates the classes with the largest margin measured using Euclidean geometry. The finding connects momentum-based optimization to the low-complexity solution preference associated with ordinary gradient descent.

The analysis also covers stochastic gradient descent with momentum and deterministic Adam, showing convergence to the L2 maximum-margin solution in the studied setting. The stochastic result relies on a new convergence analysis under an affine noise variance condition. Numerical experiments support the theory. The significance is a shared implicit bias across these optimizers under the stated classification assumptions, rather than a claim about momentum in arbitrary neural-network training.
neurips-2022-does-momentum-change-the-im.tldr: On separable linear classification with exponential-tailed loss, the analyzed momentum methods retain the L2 maximum-margin bias of gradient descent.

paragraphs: Stochastic Polyak stepsizes adapt the learning rate during stochastic gradient descent. The paper examines difficulties that arise when interpolation does not hold, including regularized objectives. In this setting, the original method needs unknown optimal minibatch losses and guarantees convergence only to a neighborhood of the solution.

Replacing optimal loss values with lower bounds addresses the information requirement. Reaching the exact solution is harder. The authors show that dependence between the adaptive stepsize and the sampled gradient can bias the expected update near a minimizer. Consequently, reducing the stepsize during training does not by itself resolve the non-convergence behavior they identify.

The proposed DecSPS modification addresses this bias and guarantees convergence to the exact minimizer without prior knowledge of problem parameters. For strongly convex problems, the authors identify it as the first stochastic adaptive optimizer with this guarantee that avoids assumptions such as bounded iterates or gradients. The contribution combines a diagnosis of why an adaptive rule can stall with a modified rule supported by exact-convergence theory.
neurips-2022-dynamics-of-sgd-with-stocha.tldr: DecSPS addresses bias in stochastic Polyak stepsizes and provides exact-convergence guarantees without prior problem-parameter knowledge.

paragraphs: Elementwise multiplication, also called a Hadamard product, appears in neural architectures whose training behavior is not fully covered by standard neural tangent kernel analyses. The paper studies polynomial neural networks as a particular class of these architectures. Its aim is to explain how multiplication affects extrapolation and the kinds of functions learned during training.

The authors derive a finite-width neural tangent kernel for polynomial networks and prove equivalence to regression using the associated kernel. This creates a mathematical route for comparing polynomial networks with standard neural networks. Their analysis shows that polynomial networks can fit more complicated functions outside the training regime and that their kernels have more slowly decaying eigenvalues.

That spectral property leads to faster learning of high-frequency functions in the analysis. The authors also explain that their theoretical results can extend to other networks with Hadamard products. Empirical results support the identified distinctions in broader architectural classes, linking the use of multiplication to specific differences in extrapolation and learning behavior.
neurips-2022-extrapolation-and-spectral-.tldr: A neural tangent kernel analysis explains how polynomial networks can extrapolate more complex functions and learn high-frequency functions faster than standard networks.

paragraphs: The densest subgraph problem seeks a densely connected part of a graph, while local decomposition provides a more detailed description of its density structure. For large graphs, simple iterative methods can work better in practice than methods built around network-flow or linear-programming solvers. This paper develops an iterative approach with improved theoretical convergence and practical scalability.

The proposed algorithm handles both problems and reaches an epsilon-additive approximation to the local decomposition vector in O(sqrt(m times maximum degree)/epsilon) iterations, where m is the edge count. Each iteration takes O(m) time. The authors also describe fractional peeling, a technique with theoretical guarantees and strong reported empirical performance.

Experiments on real and synthetic graphs show significant benefits over previous algorithms. The method is described as simple and scalable to graphs with hundreds of millions of edges. The algorithm and analysis also extend to hypergraphs, and the paper considers supermodular generalizations. Together, these results connect improved approximation guarantees with an implementation suited to large graph workloads.
neurips-2022-faster-and-scalable-algorit.tldr: A scalable iterative algorithm improves approximation guarantees for graph density problems and shows substantial empirical benefits on large graphs.

paragraphs: A probabilistic model must work on data it did not see during training. This is particularly relevant when the model supports lossless compression, where its probability estimates affect performance. The paper studies this issue in variational autoencoders, focusing on how their inference component contributes to the difference between training performance and performance on unseen examples.

The authors distinguish two generalization gaps affecting VAEs and find that amortized inference usually dominates overfitting. Amortized inference uses a shared learned procedure to perform inference across examples. The result points to the generalization of that shared procedure as a major source of the model's overall training-to-test gap in the studied setting.

Based on this diagnosis, the paper introduces a training objective intended to improve how amortized inference generalizes. The authors demonstrate performance improvements in image modeling and lossless compression. The contribution therefore links an explanation of where overfitting tends to arise with a targeted training change, rather than treating the VAE's generalization behavior as a single undifferentiated problem.
neurips-2022-generalization-gap-in-amort.tldr: The paper identifies amortized inference as a usual dominant source of VAE overfitting and proposes a training objective that improves generalization.

paragraphs: Learning from label proportions addresses a situation where examples arrive in groups and only each group's class proportions are known. Individual labels remain unavailable, yet the goal is to classify individual examples in the future. This makes the supervision indirect: the learner must extract useful classification information from aggregate descriptions.

The paper turns this problem into one of learning with noisy labels. It uses the forward correction loss to build that connection, providing a theoretically grounded approach for multiclass data. This reduction matters because it makes tools for handling unreliable labels applicable to a setting where the original supervision consists of group-level proportions.

The authors establish an excess-risk bound and analyze generalization error for their method. They also extend the theory of the forward correction loss itself. Experiments with deep-learning models across multiple datasets and architectures show improved performance over leading methods. The result combines a mathematical account of learning from aggregate supervision with evidence that the approach can improve practical individual-level classification.
neurips-2022-learning-from-label-proport.tldr: Reducing learning from label proportions to noisy-label learning yields a multiclass method with theoretical guarantees and improved empirical performance.

paragraphs: Learning broadly useful agents requires exploration that is not tied to one reward function. It also requires collecting substantial experience without repeatedly paying for centralized retraining. The paper combines these goals in a reward-free deployment efficiency setting, asking how exploration can support later tasks while using only a handful of deployments.

CASCADE collects data through a population of agents to learn a world model. Its information-theoretic objective is inspired by Bayesian active learning, and its cascading objective specifically encourages diversity among the population's trajectories. The design makes the variety of the population's collective experience an explicit part of exploration.

The authors provide theoretical intuition and demonstrate an advantage in a tabular setting over naive approaches that ignore population diversity. Across Atari, MiniGrid, Crafter, and the DM Control Suite, they also report diverse task-agnostic datasets and agents that generalize zero-shot to unseen downstream tasks. These findings support coordinating exploration around diverse experience as a route to more reusable world models and agents.
neurips-2022-learning-general-world-mode.tldr: CASCADE coordinates diverse reward-free exploration across a population to learn world models and support zero-shot transfer to unseen tasks.

paragraphs: Ensemble defenses combine several models and may train them so that attacks transfer poorly between members. The paper finds that existing attack methods can substantially overestimate the robustness of these defenses. It identifies gradient obfuscation and the diversity of member gradients as two reasons that attacks struggle to reveal weaknesses.

Simply adding gradients from all members can work against the overall attack objective. Moreover, an ensemble can make a wrong prediction even when most members remain correct. MORA addresses this by reweighting the importance of individual model gradients while constructing adversarial examples, directing the attack toward weaknesses of the combined prediction.

Across the evaluated ensembles and softmax, voting, and logit combination modes, MORA achieves higher attack success and can converge orders of magnitude faster than the compared white-box attacks. Most examined defenses have near-zero or zero robustness at the reported infinity-norm perturbation limits: 0.02 on CIFAR-10 and 0.01 on CIFAR-100. These findings concern the tested defenses and show how evaluation weaknesses can create an inflated impression of robustness.
neurips-2022-mora-improving-ensemble-rob.tldr: MORA reweights ensemble-member gradients to expose substantial robustness overestimation in the evaluated ensemble defenses.

paragraphs: In sequential prediction, a learner assigns probabilities as observations arrive and incurs logarithmic loss. The paper studies how much extra loss the learner must suffer relative to the best expert in a specified class. This difference is regret, and minimax regret describes the best achievable worst-case performance.

The authors derive a general upper bound and then study particular expert classes, including those constrained by Lipschitz regularity or bounded Hessians. For these classes, they obtain matching lower and upper bounds with provably optimal constants. The bounds apply across a wide range of data dimensions and numbers of prediction rounds.

The lower bounds use information-theoretic tools, while the upper bounds rely on a new smooth truncated covering of the expert class. This construction supports a simple truncated Bayesian algorithm, making the upper-bound argument constructive. The authors report simpler proofs and tighter, often optimal bounds. Matching bounds matter because they identify both what an algorithm can achieve and what no algorithm can improve upon in the specified setting.
neurips-2022-precise-regret-bounds-for-l.tldr: A truncated Bayesian algorithm yields constructive log-loss regret bounds that often match lower bounds, including optimal constants for specified expert classes.

paragraphs: Single-cell measurements reveal how individual cells respond differently to a drug, but measuring these responses for many drugs is technically difficult and expensive. Bulk RNA screening data are more routinely available. The paper investigates how information from those existing screens can improve predictions at the level of individual cells.

The authors introduce chemCPA, an encoder-decoder architecture designed to study responses to drugs that were not seen during training. They combine it with an architectural modification for transfer learning, allowing training on existing bulk RNA screening datasets to inform the single-cell prediction task. The reported finding is that this transfer improves generalization.

Better prediction of unseen drug effects can reduce the need for extensive single-cell screening. The authors envision using the model to generate computational hypotheses and guide more efficient experiments, with the longer-term aim of accelerating drug discovery. That prospective application is distinct from the demonstrated finding: the abstract establishes improved generalization through bulk-data transfer, while presenting improved experimental design as an intended use.
neurips-2022-predicting-cellular-respons.tldr: chemCPA transfers information from bulk RNA screens to improve generalization when predicting single-cell responses to unseen drugs.

paragraphs: Some prediction problems contain genuine ambiguity: the same RNA sequence can fold into different structures. Measurements can introduce additional variation through noise or differences in technique. The paper argues that a model should represent these distributions of possibilities, giving it probabilistic characteristics suited to the data it is asked to learn.

The proposed Probabilistic Transformer adds a hierarchical latent distribution to the transformer architecture. This provides a way to represent hidden variability within the model. The authors evaluate the approach on a synthetic task designed to test whether it can learn an underlying data distribution, alongside two scientific applications.

For RNA folding, they report state-of-the-art results and particular advantages on highly ambiguous data. For molecule design conditioned on desired properties, they demonstrate generative capabilities and performance exceeding existing work through implicit learning of the underlying distributions. Together, these findings support incorporating structured probabilistic representations into transformers when multiple outcomes and variation are central features of the task.
neurips-2022-probabilistic-transformer-m.tldr: A transformer enhanced with hierarchical latent distributions improves modeling of ambiguous RNA structures and property-based molecule generation.

paragraphs: Wearable sensors can monitor physiology frequently during daily life, potentially supporting precisely timed health interventions. Missing measurements are a major obstacle. The paper focuses on filling gaps in pulsative signals, whose repeating pulse structure makes them a challenging target for existing imputation methods.

PulseImpute provides a large-scale benchmark for this problem. It combines realistic models of missing data in mobile health with a broad set of baseline methods and clinically relevant downstream tasks. These components bring together the conditions under which data disappear, methods for reconstructing them, and tasks that make the reconstruction useful.

The baseline collection includes a new transformer architecture designed to exploit the structure of pulsative signals. The paper's central contribution is the benchmark and its accompanying methods, addressing the shortage of available datasets that has hindered progress. Its stated aim is to enable further machine-learning research on physiological signal imputation; the abstract does not present the benchmark as an already demonstrated improvement in patient outcomes.
neurips-2022-pulseimpute-a-novel-benchma.tldr: PulseImpute supplies a large-scale benchmark, realistic missingness models, and baselines for reconstructing missing pulsative physiological signals.

paragraphs: Requiring generated text to contain particular words does not ensure that those words express the intended relationship. A sentence can include all requested terms while getting its grammar or facts wrong. The paper introduces relation-constrained decoding, where output must contain specified word pairs connected by specified relations.

Its RESEAL algorithm guides generation through probability adjustments and beam allocation. It can handle different kinds of relations, including syntactic and factual ones, and adaptively assembles those relations into a sentence. The method is designed as a plug-and-play addition at inference time for autoregressive text generators.

The authors build a benchmark from treebanks with annotated grammatical dependencies and show better preservation of input dependency relations than previous methods. They also apply RESEAL to summarization, fact-based text editing, and data-to-text generation, reporting improved generation quality. These results support making relationships explicit in decoding, so that control concerns how requested words connect as well as whether they appear.
neurips-2022-relation-constrained-decodi.tldr: RESEAL guides autoregressive text generation to preserve specified relationships between words, improving relation preservation and quality in evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Adversarial team games combine cooperation within a team with competition against opponents. Team members may have different information, which makes approximating equilibrium strategies computationally difficult. This paper extends a successful approach from two-player zero-sum games: prepare an approximate blueprint strategy offline, then refine the relevant part while the game is being played.

The method uses a team belief directed acyclic graph to construct an auxiliary gadget game. It then refines the blueprint through column generation, adding strategy components as needed. The process is anytime, allowing refinement to proceed according to the computation available during play.

The computational guarantee has two explicit conditions: the blueprint must be sparse, and a best-response oracle must be available. Under those conditions, the complete algorithm runs in polynomial time and avoids expanding the full team belief graph, whose worst-case size is exponential. Experiments on a standard test suite show improved strategy performance from subgame solving. The contribution is an online refinement method for team games with both conditional scalability guarantees and empirical support.
neurips-2022-subgame-solving-in-adversar.tldr: An online subgame-solving method improves team-game strategies and runs in polynomial time given a sparse blueprint and a best-response oracle.

paragraphs: Tensor decompositions represent high-dimensional arrays through interacting smaller factors. More elaborate tensor-network structures can improve recovery of missing data, but they also introduce many rank settings to choose. The paper addresses this growing hyperparameter burden, particularly when the data have many dimensions.

Tensor wheel decomposition arranges latent factors in a wheel-shaped network. The design starts from analysis of the graph structure, aiming to capture complex interactions while keeping the number of hyperparameters lower. The authors argue theoretically that this organization alleviates the difficulties associated with increasingly intricate tensor-network models.

To demonstrate the decomposition, the paper applies it to tensor completion, the recovery of missing entries. It develops an efficient solver based on proximal alternating minimization and provides a convergence guarantee. Experiments on synthetic and real data report significantly better performance than other state-of-the-art tensor-decomposition methods. These findings support the wheel topology as a useful representation for the tested recovery problems, pairing its structural design with a concrete optimization procedure.
neurips-2022-tensor-wheel-decomposition-.tldr: Tensor wheel decomposition uses a wheel-shaped factor network to limit hyperparameter complexity and improve tensor completion in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Larger batches and learning rates can shorten language-model training, but they can also destabilize it. The authors study GPT-2 replications and find a strong correlation between instability and extreme gradient variance. Long sequences contribute to those extreme values, especially early in training, suggesting sequence length as a useful control.

Sequence Length Warmup begins with shorter sequences and increases their length during training. The paper also offers a lightweight tuning strategy using a small portion of a full run. In GPT-2 replications with 117 million and 1.5 billion parameters, the method supports eightfold larger batches and fourfold larger learning rates while maintaining stability. Comparable or better zero-shot results require up to 2.2 times fewer tokens and 3.7 times less time.

In a 125-million-parameter GPT-3 replication, it supports eightfold larger batches and fortyfold larger learning rates. It retains 99% of zero-shot accuracy across 11 tasks using tenfold less data and seventeenfold less time than the original recipe. These experimental findings connect early sequence-length control with more efficient, stable training in the evaluated configurations.
neurips-2022-the-stability-efficiency-di.tldr: Sequence Length Warmup stabilizes the evaluated GPT training runs at larger batches and learning rates, substantially reducing data and time requirements.

paragraphs: Best-arm identification asks which option has the highest expected reward, with a specified level of confidence. Top-two algorithms collect evidence by randomizing between two candidates: a leader and a challenger. Although these methods perform well empirically, earlier fixed-confidence guarantees were restricted to Gaussian rewards with known variances.

The paper develops a general analysis that separates the properties needed from the leader, the challenger, and the reward distributions. This makes it possible to reason about top-two methods beyond that Gaussian setting, including distributions that need not belong to a specified parametric family.

The analysis yields theoretically supported algorithms for bounded reward distributions. It also shows that the leader-selection step inherited from Thompson sampling can be replaced by other choices, including selecting the option with the highest observed average reward. This matters because it identifies flexibility within the top-two design: the theoretical support can apply to a broader family of candidate-selection procedures, rather than depending on that particular sampling step.
neurips-2022-top-two-algorithms-revisite.tldr: A general analysis extends theoretical support for top-two best-arm identification to bounded distributions and alternative leader-selection rules.

paragraphs: Image-generating autoencoders need to produce convincing images and learn representations that withstand adversarial perturbations. The paper explores deterministic autoencoders as an alternative to variational autoencoders, whose vulnerability has been associated with their variational formulation. Its goal is to improve robustness without sacrificing generated-image quality.

The proposed method adds a regularization scheme that incorporates adversarially perturbed examples during training. Its loss compares representations using a two-point Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. According to the abstract, this scheme does not increase computational complexity or compromise generation fidelity, making the representation-level comparison central to the proposed combination of robustness and quality.

The authors evaluate the approach on popular image benchmarks using attacks targeted at variational autoencoders. Their empirical findings show strong performance in both robustness and fidelity compared with robust VAE models. The significance is that the evaluated deterministic approach improves both goals together. The evidence supports this result for the reported comparisons, rather than establishing resistance to every possible attack.
neurips-2022-trading-off-image-quality-f.tldr: A representation-based regularizer gives deterministic autoencoders improved adversarial robustness and image fidelity in comparisons with robust VAEs.

paragraphs: A benchmark needs a rule for combining performance across tasks as well as datasets and metrics. Averaging scores is common, but metrics with different scales can distort the resulting comparison. This paper examines how the aggregation rule affects which language-processing systems appear best.

The authors propose ranking systems within each task and then combining those rankings into an overall ordering. Motivated by social choice theory, the procedure has a theoretical foundation. Its focus on task-level rankings changes how heterogeneous performance measures contribute to the final comparison, directly addressing problems associated with averaging scores on different scales.

The evaluation uses more than 270,000 synthetic and real scores, including results from several established benchmarks. The authors find that their procedure can produce different conclusions about state-of-the-art systems while being more reliable and robust than mean aggregation. The contribution shows that benchmark conclusions depend partly on how evidence across tasks is combined, making aggregation itself an important component of evaluation design.
neurips-2022-what-are-the-best-systems-n.tldr: Aggregating task-level rankings offers a theoretically grounded alternative to averaging benchmark scores, with more reliable and robust reported comparisons.
